967.title: Cyril, Methodius and Valentine (14 February)
967.hook: the calendar keeps the brothers of the Slavs on the same day as Valentine, a Roman martyr
967.howItsDone: Catholics in the Roman calendar keep 14 February as the memorial of Saints Cyril and Methodius, patrons of Europe, while Valentine is remembered in the Roman Martyrology; Slavic Catholic and Orthodox communities celebrate the brothers with special honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Apollonia of Alexandria, the older woman who would not deny Christ before a mob. Your line was she kept faith.

Shop windows on the fourteenth of February: red hearts, roses in plastic sleeves, cards with a little winged boy and his bow. Open the Church's calendar to the same square, and the first names printed there are two brothers from the Greek world who gave a people an alphabet: Cyril and Methodius. Somewhere below them, in the old list of martyrs, is a Roman called Valentine. So the day holds two gifts side by side. Love, and letters.
screen: `HEARTS IN THE SHOP WINDOW.` → `TWO BROTHERS IN THE CALENDAR.` → `LOVE, AND LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the brothers grew up in Thessalonica, in Greece, and were sent north to the Slavic peoples, who had no written form of their own language. Preaching to someone in a borrowed language is like singing a song in a key they can't reach. So the brothers did something patient and strange: they built an alphabet. With it they translated the Gospels and the prayers of the liturgy into the people's own Slavonic speech. Not everyone liked it. Tradition says some churchmen argued that worship belonged only in the old sacred languages, so the brothers traveled to Rome to make their case, and the pope received them and let the Slavonic books be used. Cyril, the younger, died in Rome. Methodius went back and kept working. A line in the Acts of the Apostles, from Pentecost, sounds like their whole life. In the Douay-Rheims, the crowd says: "we have heard them speak in our own tongues the wonderful works of God." The Church remembers them as apostles of the Slavs and keeps them among the patron saints of Europe. And Valentine? Honestly, very little is known. He is remembered as a Roman martyr. The hearts, the cards and the birds pairing off came later, from customs and poems, not from anything we know of his life. Still, the two belong on one day: to give someone words in their own language is a way of loving them.

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind and ask what their language is: some people hear love in words, some in a cooked meal, a fixed bike, or a message that just says thinking of you. Choose the thing they'd understand, not the thing easiest for you to give. If you pray, hold them before God for a moment; if you don't, just keep their face in mind.
Cyril. With his brother Methodius, the apostle of the Slavs, who gave a people letters for their own language so they could hear the Gospel in it.
Your line: love and letters. Two kinds of gift on one February day. That's day nine hundred sixty-seven.

968.title: The martyrs of Libya (15 February)
968.hook: Coptic Christians killed on a beach in Libya, now honored in the Roman Martyrology
968.howItsDone: The Coptic Orthodox Church keeps these men as martyrs and saints on 15 February, and since their inclusion in the Roman Martyrology Catholics also remember them that day, often praying for Christians who suffer for their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyril and Methodius, who gave a people an alphabet for their own tongue. Your line was love and letters.

Today's saints were not from long ago. They were workers, in our own time: men who had left their villages in Egypt to find jobs in Libya and send money home to their families. They were kidnapped by an armed group, dressed in orange, led onto a beach by the sea, and killed. Their killers filmed it and sent the film around the world. Reports of the film say that, at the end, some of the men were heard calling on Jesus. The Church remembers them as the martyrs of Libya.
screen: `WORKERS FAR FROM HOME.` → `A BEACH, AND A FILM.` → `CALLING ON JESUS.`

segments.voice: Almost all the men were Coptic Orthodox Christians, from the ancient Church of Egypt. One who died with them was from Ghana, and tradition among the Copts holds that he chose to stand with the others. Here's what makes this day unusual in a Catholic calendar. The Coptic Orthodox Church is not in full communion with Rome. It has its own pope in Alexandria, its own liturgy, its own saints. Their pope declared these men martyrs and saints of his Church. Later, Pope Francis received the Coptic pope at the Vatican and announced that the men would be added to the Roman Martyrology, the Catholic Church's official list of saints and martyrs. A Church honoring martyrs who were not its own members, because of how they died. Pope Francis had a phrase for this: an ecumenism of blood. Those who kill Christians, he said in effect, don't stop to ask which church they belong to. Catholics and Copts still differ on real questions, and both say so. But in the Martyrology, the names stand together. In the Greek of the Acts of the Apostles, the word for witnesses is the word English borrowed as martyr. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells his followers, "you shall be witnesses unto me," and sends that witness to the uttermost part of the earth. A beach in Libya is one of those far places. These men preached no sermon there. Their witness was a name on their lips.

segments.voice: Bring to mind the families in those villages who sent their sons out to work and waited for calls that stopped coming, then widen it to Coptic Christians today, in Egypt and in cities all over the world, getting up for church, raising children, burying their dead. If you pray, hold them before God in your own words or with the Lord's Prayer; if you don't, give one breath to the families and one to the men.

Ecumenism. Pope Francis's word for what unites Catholics and Copts killed for Christ: the Coptic Christians of this day, killed on a Libyan beach, declared saints by their own Church and added to the Catholic Martyrology.

969.title: Jacinta and Francisco Marto (20 February)
969.hook: two of the Fatima children, a brother and sister who died young and were canonized together
969.howItsDone: Catholics keep 20 February as the memorial of Saints Francisco and Jacinta Marto, especially in Portugal, and pilgrims visit their tombs at the shrine of Fatima, often praying the rosary there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the martyrs of Libya, Coptic workers whose names now stand in the Roman Martyrology. Your line was the twenty-one.

A hillside in Portugal, sheep grazing, three children with a packed lunch and a long afternoon. Lucia, the oldest, and her two younger cousins, a brother and sister named Francisco and Jacinta Marto. They're supposed to say the rosary while they watch the flock, and, by Lucia's own later account, they sometimes rushed it, saying just the first words of each prayer so they could get back to their games. Then, the children said, a lady brighter than the sun appeared to them above a small tree.
screen: `THREE CHILDREN AND A FLOCK.` → `A RUSHED ROSARY.` → `A LADY ABOVE A SMALL TREE.`

segments.voice: Fatima is famous for the visions: a lady the children understood to be Mary, messages about prayer and penance, a crowd watching the sky. The Church judged those events worthy of belief, its careful phrase. Private revelations like Fatima are not part of the faith Catholics are required to hold; Catholics are free to weigh them. But that's not why Jacinta and Francisco are saints. The Church canonizes people for how they lived, and these two lived differently afterward. Francisco was the quiet one. Lucia remembered him slipping into the parish church to sit near the tabernacle for hours, keeping company with the hidden Jesus, as he called him. He wanted, he said, to console God. Jacinta was the fierce one. She took the call to penance seriously, giving her lunch to poorer children and offering up small hardships for sinners. Not long after the visions, both children fell seriously ill. Francisco died at home. Jacinta died in a hospital in Lisbon, far from her family. They were still children. Pope Francis canonized them together at Fatima. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus prays: "thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones." In naming these two, the Church took him at his word. Holiness was not waiting for them to grow up.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a child you know who is unwell, or the children in a hospital near you tonight, with the parents beside the beds and the nurses on the late shift. You don't need words; just keep them company, the way Francisco sat with the hidden Jesus. If you pray, offer them to God, perhaps with a Hail Mary; if you don't, give each one a slow breath.

970.title: Peter Damian (21 February)
970.hook: a monk and reformer who wrote blunt letters against corruption in the Church
970.howItsDone: Catholics keep 21 February as the memorial of Saint Peter Damian, bishop and Doctor of the Church, and his letters and writings on prayer are read in the Liturgy of the Hours and by those interested in Church reform.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jacinta and Francisco Marto, the children of Fatima, saints for how they lived. Your line was the children of fatima.

Some letters you write three times. The first draft is furious. The second is so polite it says nothing. The third, if you're lucky, says the true thing plainly, because you care about the person reading it. Peter Damian spent much of his life writing the third kind. A monk in Italy who loved silence and his hermit's cell, he kept being pulled out of it to tell bishops, priests and even popes what they did not want to hear. He signed himself, tradition says, Peter the sinner, monk.
screen: `THREE DRAFTS OF A HARD LETTER.` → `A MONK PULLED FROM HIS CELL.` → `PETER THE SINNER, MONK.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Peter Damian began poor. An orphan, he was taken in by relatives and set to work as a boy looking after pigs, until an older brother saw how bright he was and paid for his schooling. He became a teacher, then left it all for a hermitage, where the monks lived in small cells and prayed through the night. He would have stayed. But the Church of his day was sick in ways that were hard to miss. Church offices were bought and sold, a corruption known as simony. Clergy were living double lives. Peter wrote letters that named things plainly, and the popes kept calling him to help with reform. He was made a cardinal and bishop and, tradition says, asked more than once to go back to his cell. What makes him worth remembering isn't just that he was blunt. Plenty of people are. It's that he aimed the same honesty at himself. That signature was not a pose. The book of Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims, has a line for this kind of friend: "Better are the wounds of a friend, than the deceitful kisses of an enemy." His letters could wound. He wrote them because he loved the Church, not to win. The Church later named him a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone. Blunt love tells the truth, includes itself in the problem, and stays to help fix it.
screen: `A SWINEHERD BOY, THEN A HERMIT.` · `A CHURCH SELLING ITS OFFICES.` · `BLUNT LETTERS, AND BLUNT WITH HIMSELF.` · `CALLED TO HELP, LONGING FOR HIS CELL.` · then, large: `BETTER ARE THE WOUNDS OF A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing that's gone a little crooked, at work, in a group you belong to, or in your own habits, and name it privately in plain words, the way Peter Damian would. Then do what he did with his signature: find your own part in it, however small. If you pray, bring it to God and ask for the courage to say it kindly; if you don't, let it sit, named, while you breathe.

971.title: Gregory of Narek (27 February)
971.hook: an Armenian monk whose Book of Lamentations is a conversation with God from the depths
971.howItsDone: Armenian Christians, both Apostolic and Catholic, honor Saint Gregory of Narek, and some families keep his Book of Lamentations at home for prayer, especially in illness; in the Roman calendar he is remembered on 27 February.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Damian, the monk who wrote hard letters to popes and signed himself a sinner. Your line was blunt love.

In some Armenian homes there's a book kept near the bed, or tucked under the pillow of someone who is sick. It's a book of prayers, and people often call it simply by its author's village: the Narek. Tradition says families read from it at bedsides and in hard nights, the way others keep a rosary in a pocket. Its author was a monk at a monastery called Narek, by a lake in Armenia, long ago. His book starts from the bottom.
screen: `A BOOK UNDER THE PILLOW.` → `THEY CALL IT THE NAREK.` → `A MONK BY A LAKE.`

segments.voice: Gregory called his book a Book of Lamentations. Each of its prayers, by tradition, opens with the same phrase, which can be put in English as speaking with God from the depths of the heart. Gregory doesn't write as a holy man explaining prayer to beginners. He writes as someone who has looked honestly at himself and doesn't like all he sees. He piles up images for his own brokenness: a ship breaking apart, a field gone to weeds, a debtor with nothing to pay. Page after page, he refuses to pretend. And then, again and again, he turns: not to his own goodness, which he's just given up on, but to God's mercy, which he trusts more than his own despair. He even prays for the people who will read him, and for those who wrong him. That shape is old; the Psalms have it. In the Douay-Rheims, the psalm Catholics know as the De profundis begins: "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord: Lord, hear my voice." Gregory's book reads like that first line, carried across page after page. He belongs first to the Armenian Apostolic Church, which honors him as a saint. Armenian Catholics honor him too, and Pope Francis named him a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Catholic Church. A monk who wrote so honestly about how lost he was became a teacher. Prayer doesn't have to start from the top.
screen: `SPEAKING WITH GOD FROM THE DEPTHS.` · `HONEST ABOUT HIS OWN BROKENNESS.` · `THEN TURNING TO MERCY.` · `AN ARMENIAN DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE DEPTHS I HAVE CRIED TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Let one honest thing rise, something you're carrying that isn't tidy, a failure, a fear, a grudge, a tiredness, and don't dress it up or argue it down. Then turn, the way Gregory does: if you pray, say the psalm's first line, out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord, and leave the rest to God. If you don't, breathe out slowly and let the heavy thing sit beside you rather than on top of you.

972.title: Casimir (4 March)
972.hook: a young Polish prince who turned back from a war and gave to the poor
972.howItsDone: Catholics keep 4 March as the memorial of Saint Casimir, with special celebrations in Lithuania and Poland, where pilgrims visit his chapel in Vilnius cathedral and a traditional Kaziukas fair is held in Vilnius around his feast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory of Narek, the Armenian monk who spoke with God from the depths of the heart. Your line was the book of lamentations.

A young prince rides at the head of an army. His father, the king of Poland, has sent him to take a neighboring crown, the crown of Hungary, which some nobles there have offered him. Banners, horses, the whole weight of a dynasty behind him. And partway there, the prince turns around and goes home. Tradition gives more than one reason: soldiers deserting for lack of pay, a pope against the war, a rival king already holding the throne. But the Church remembers what the prince did with that moment. His name was Casimir.
screen: `A YOUNG PRINCE AT THE HEAD OF AN ARMY.` → `A CROWN ON OFFER.` → `HE TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: The story goes that his father was furious and sent him away from court for a while. Casimir would not be talked into marching again. Whatever the full mix of reasons, his biographers tell it as a matter of conscience, and he never changed his mind. What he did instead is the part they lingered on. He lived plainly inside a palace. Tradition says he slept on the floor, rose at night to pray at church doors before they opened, and gave his own money to the poor, the sick and pilgrims, so freely that he became known as their defender. He loved Mary deeply, and tradition says he loved a Latin hymn that begins Omni die dic Mariae, daily, daily, sing to Mary, and that a copy was buried with him. He fell ill with a lung disease and died young, before he ever ruled anything. He is buried in the cathedral in Vilnius, and Lithuania and Poland both claim him as a patron. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says on the mountain: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Casimir was a king's son who chose to be remembered as one of those children instead. Refusing a fight is not always the easy road. For a prince, it meant his father's anger, a lost crown, and a quiet life the court didn't understand.

segments.voice: Find one fight you're in or about to be in, an argument you're rehearsing, a group chat you're ready to win, and ask whether it's worth marching for. 973.title: John of God (8 March)
973.hook: a former soldier and bookseller who began caring for the sick, and whose followers became a hospital order
973.howItsDone: Catholics keep 8 March as the memorial of Saint John of God, patron of hospitals, nurses and the sick, and the Hospitaller Order he inspired runs hospitals and care homes that mark the day with Mass and celebrations for patients and staff.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Casimir, the prince who turned his army around and gave his money to the poor. Your line was the prince who refused.

A street in Granada, in Spain. A man who sells holy books and pictures from a little shop stands in a crowd listening to the preacher John of Avila. Something in the sermon breaks him open. He runs through the streets crying out for mercy, tearing up his own books, giving away everything in the shop. The neighbors decide he has lost his mind, and he's taken to the city hospital and locked in the ward for the mad. That ward is where his story really begins. The Church calls him John of God.
screen: `A BOOKSELLER IN GRANADA.` → `A SERMON BREAKS HIM OPEN.` → `LOCKED IN THE WARD FOR THE MAD.`

segments.voice: Before Granada, tradition says, John had been a shepherd, a soldier and a drifter, and none of it had gone well. Inside, he saw what was done to people judged insane: on that ward, tradition says, they were beaten to drive the madness out, and so was John. He made a decision there: if he ever got out, he would care for the sick the way he wished someone had cared for him and the men beside him. John of Avila came to visit and calmed him, and once released, John did exactly that. He rented a house, filled it with the sick and the homeless, and went out at night with a basket, begging for them. Tradition says his cry in the streets was, roughly, do good, brothers, to yourselves: helping the poor was a gift to the giver. He washed patients, carried them on his back, and sorted them by need. The bishop, tradition says, gave him the name John of God. After his death his helpers carried on and became the Hospitaller Brothers of Saint John of God, a religious order devoted to the sick. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus describes the judgment, and kindness done to him in the least of people: "sick, and you visited me: I was in prison, and you came to me." John had been both. A man once treated as mad became a patron of hospitals and the sick.
screen: `SHEPHERD, SOLDIER, DRIFTER, BOOKSELLER.` · `BEATEN ON THE WARD FOR THE MAD.` · `A RENTED HOUSE AND A BASKET AT NIGHT.` · `HIS HELPERS BECOME AN ORDER.` · then, large: `SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who is ill, or worn out caring for someone who is, and ask what would actually go in John's night basket for them: not flowers, but soup, a lift to an appointment, an hour so the carer can sleep. If you pray, pray for them and those who care for them; if you don't, keep them in mind as you breathe.
Granada, the Spanish city where John of God, once locked up as mad, began caring for the sick, and whose helpers became the Hospitaller Brothers.
